function.name: calc_heat_capacity
function.description: Calculate the heat capacity at constant pressure of air using its temperature and volume. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

temp.description: The temperature of the gas in Kelvin.

volume.description: The volume of the gas in m^3.

gas.description: Type of gas, with air as default.

function.name: calculate_discounted_cash_flow
function.description: Calculate the discounted cash flow of a bond for a given annual coupon payment, time frame and discount rate. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

coupon_payment.description: The annual coupon payment. This is a float type value.

period.description: The time frame in years for which coupon payment is made.

discount_rate.description: The discount rate. This is a float type value.

face_value.description: The face value of the bond, default is $1000.

message.content:
**Step‑by‑step calculation**

| Symbol | Value | Units |
|--------|-------|-------|
| \(T\) | 298 | K |
| \(V\) | 10 | m³ |
| \(p\) | 101 325 | Pa (assumed atmospheric pressure) |

---

### 1. Determine how much “air” is inside the 10 m³ container  

For an **ideal gas**  
\(n=\dfrac{PV}{RT}\)

where  
\(R = 8.314\, \text{J mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\).

Plugging in:

\[
n=
\dfrac{(101\,325)(10)}{(8.314)(298)}
\simeq 
\dfrac{1\,013\,250}{2\,477.9}
\simeq 409.3\;\text{mol}
\]

So roughly **410 mol** of air occupy this space under normal conditions.

> ⚠️ If you have a different pressure than 1 atm, replace it accordingly – the result scales linearly with pressure.

---

### 2. Heat capacity at constant pressure (\(C_p\))

Air behaves approximately like a diatomic molecule mixture (mostly N₂ & O₂).  
Its **molar heat capacity at constant pressure** near room temperature is

\[
C_{p,\text{molar}}\approx 29\;\text{J mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}.
\]

Total heat capacity:

\[
C_p=n\,C_{p,\text{molar}}
   =(409.3)\,(29)
   \simeq 11\,870\;\text{J K}^{-1}.
\]

Rounded to three significant figures:
\[
\boxed{C_p \approx 1.19\times10^{4}\;\text{J K}^{-1}} .
\]

---

#### Alternative view – Specific heat per kilogram

Specific heat of dry air at constant pressure:

\[
c_{p,\text{specific}}\approx 1005\;\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}.
\]

Mass contained in 10 m³ at sea‑level density (~1.225 kg m⁻³):

\[
m=p\rho V = 1.225\times10 = 12.25\;\text{kg},
\]
so

\[
C_p=m\,c_{p,\text{specific}}
     =(12.25)(1005)
     \approx 12\,300\;\text{J K}^{-1},
\]

which agrees closely with the molar approach once rounding differences are considered.

---

### Summary

Under ordinary laboratory conditions (ambient pressure, 298 K), the heat capacity at constant pressure of the 10 m³ sample of air is **about 1.2×10⁴ J K⁻¹**.  
If your system operates at a different pressure, simply scale the result proportionally—heat capacity ∝ pressure when all other variables stay fixed.
message.reasoning:
The user wants to compute the heat capacity at constant pressure (Cp) of air at T=298 K, V=10 m³. They didn't specify units or method; we can use ideal gas assumption? But Cp depends on specific heats per mole or mass. For an ideal diatomic gas like N2/O2 mixture approximating air, Cp ≈ 29 J/(mol·K). However they gave volume but not amount of substance. We need either molar quantity or mass.

We could assume standard conditions: 1 atm, 298 K, so density ~1.225 kg/m³. So mass in 10 m³ is about 12.25 kg. Moles: n = PV/RT. P=101325 Pa, R=8.3145 J/mol/K. Compute n = (P*V)/(R*T)=?

Let's do calculation quickly: P*V = 101325 * 10 = 1,013,250 Pa*m³ = Joules? Actually 1 Pa*m³ = 1 J. So numerator = 1,013,250 J. Denominator R*T = 8.3145 * 298 = 2477.9 J/mol. So n≈409.3 mol. That seems low because 10 m³ contains many molecules. Wait check: At STP, one mole occupies 22.414 L (~0.0224 m³), so 10 m³ would contain ~446 mol. Yes close. Good.

Now Cp_molar ~29 J/(mol*K). Then total Cp_total = n*Cpmol = 409.3 * 29 ≈ 11870 J/K. Alternatively if want per unit mass: cp_specific = Cpmol / M_air where M_air~28.97 g/mol -> convert to kg: 0.02897 kg/mol. So cp_specific = 29 / 0.02897 ≈ 1000 J/kg/K. That's typical cp of dry air ~1005 J/kg/K. Multiply by mass 12.25 kg gives same result ~12250 J/K. Slight difference due to rounding.

Thus answer: around 1.18e4 J/K. Provide explanation.

Also mention assumptions: ideal gas, composition of air etc. Use formula: Cp = n * Cp,molar. Or use cp_specific times mass.

We'll provide step-by-step calculations. Also note that volume alone insufficient without pressure; assuming atmospheric pressure. We'll show both methods.
